quickAnswer: İğneada Floodplain Forests National Park sits roughly 225 to 250 km northwest of Istanbul in Kırklareli Province, taking about 3 to 3.5 hours by car. One of Europe's rare coastal floodplain ecosystems, it combines five freshwater lakes, canoeing through flooded ash and oak corridors, wide Black Sea beaches, and forest glamping—best visited in May–June or September–October.

body.text: How far is İğneada from Istanbul by car?

İğneada is approximately 225 to 250 km northwest of central Istanbul—roughly 3 to 3.5 hours by car depending on European-side exit traffic ([İğneada Canoeing & Travel Guide](https://traveltourshop.com/blog/igneada-longoz-forests-canoeing-guide); [Rome2Rio Istanbul to İğneada](https://www.rome2rio.com/s/Istanbul/%C4%B0%C4%9Fneada-Floodplain-Forests-National-Park)). Drivers follow the TEM or Northern Marmara highway west, exit toward Saray or Çerkezköy, and continue through Vize and Demirköy over the forested Istranca (Yıldız) Mountains.

The final 60 kilometers through Demirköy wind through dense beech and oak forest, so daylight driving is strongly preferable, especially in autumn fog or wet weather. Direct buses run from Istanbul's Esenler Otogar to İğneada town, taking around 4.5 hours, but without your own vehicle it is hard to reach the national park trailheads, Erikli Lake, Beğendik beach, or Dupnisa Cave on the return route.
When is canoeing in the flooded forest best?

Late April through June is the prime window for canoeing inside İğneada's flooded forest, when spring snowmelt and rain from the Istranca Mountains keep Mert Lake and Erikli Lake high enough to paddle directly under submerged ash, alder, and oak canopies. September and October also offer calm water and golden foliage, though summer evaporation lowers inner-forest channels.

[İğneada Floodplain Forests National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%B0%C4%9Fneada_Floodplain_Forests_National_Park) protects coastal dunes, marshes, seasonally inundated woodlands, and five main lakes—Mert, Erikli, Hamam, Saka, and Pedina—recording around 670 plant species and 194 bird species ([GoTürkiye Kırklareli](https://goturkiye.com/tr/kirklareli/dokun)). Guided canoe launches operate from the mouth of Mert Lake just south of İğneada center; booking an early 08:00 AM slot rewards paddlers with glassy water, kingfishers, and herons before weekend groups arrive.
What Black Sea beaches and glamping stays exist nearby?

İğneada stretches along a wide, sandy Black Sea coastline backed by dunes and forest rather than concrete hotels. Main swimming spots include İğneada Public Beach, quieter Limanköy Cove below the historic lighthouse, and Beğendik Village Beach ten kilometers north right beside the Bulgarian border. For upscale outdoor lodging, [Longosphere Glamping](https://www.booking.com/hotel/tr/longosphere-glamping.html) offers furnished forest tents and spa facilities near town.

Because the Black Sea here faces open northerly fetch, always check daily wave and rip-current flags before swimming—calm mornings can turn choppy by mid-afternoon. Alongside Longosphere Glamping and boutique stays like Nayu İğneada, independent campers use designated sites near Mert Lake and Limanköy, while families seeking traditional hotels stay near the central waterfront close to local Black Sea fish restaurants serving seasonal turbot (kalkan), bluefish, and fried anchovies.
Which months avoid mosquitoes and winter rain?

May through mid-June and September through mid-October offer the cleanest balance of mild daytime temperatures, navigable trails, and low insect pressure. Mid-July through August brings humid heat and heavy mosquito activity around standing marsh water, while November through March delivers cold Black Sea winds, persistent rain, and deep mud across unpaved forest tracks.

items: Pack waterproof hiking shoes or light trail boots; forest dirt tracks stay muddy even days after rain.
Bring DEET or picaridin insect repellent and long sleeves for sunset walks near Mert and Erikli lakes.
Reserve Mert Lake canoe slots and Longosphere Glamping tents at least two weeks ahead for spring and autumn weekends.
Download offline maps for the Istranca Mountains and park trails, as mobile signal drops inside dense canopy zones.
Stop at Dupnisa Cave near Sarpdere Village on your drive back toward Istanbul (open seasonally; verify hours before detouring).

faq.q: Is there an entrance fee for İğneada Floodplain Forests National Park?
faq.a: Pedestrian access to the outer trails is typically free, while vehicle entry and designated camping areas carry modest national park fees collected at gated points during active season.

faq.q: Can you swim in the lakes inside İğneada Longoz?
faq.a: No. The five lakes—Mert, Erikli, Hamam, Saka, and Pedina—are protected freshwater and lagoon habitats. Visitors swim in the Black Sea along İğneada Beach, Limanköy, or Beğendik instead.

faq.q: How long should you stay in İğneada?
faq.a: Two days and one night is ideal from Istanbul: drive up Saturday morning, paddle Mert Lake in the afternoon, walk the national park trails or visit Beğendik on Sunday morning, and stop at Dupnisa Cave on the drive home.

faq.q: Are the trails inside the national park easy to follow?
faq.a: The main gravel and boardwalk stretches near Mert Lake and the 12-meter bird-watching tower are straightforward, though deeper dirt tracks toward Hamam and Pedina lakes become muddy and poorly marked after rain—go with a local guide if venturing far inside.

faq.q: Is İğneada close to the Bulgarian border?
faq.a: Yes. Beğendik Village, 10 km north of İğneada center, sits directly across the Rezovo (Mutludere) river mouth from Bulgaria, though there is no road border crossing there; travelers crossing into Bulgaria use the Dereköy border gate inland.

faq.q: Is İğneada suitable for families with young children?
faq.a: Yes. The flat forest boardwalks, gentle guided double-canoe rides on Mert Lake, and wide sandy beaches work well for families, provided children wear life jackets on the water and avoid rough Black Sea surf days.
